video.title: The #1 Backscratch Mistake — and How to Fix It

classification.reason: The coach provides executable drills and progression cues, including exploring forearm pronation/supination in front of the body, rotating the forearm above the head without a ball, and tossing a ball over the head to 'bop' it with forearm rotation.

problem.title_as_question: Why do players get stuck in the back scratch position on the serve, and how should it be fixed?
problem.definition: Players treat the back scratch position as the maximum power launch point and jackknife the racket straight up toward the ball, failing to let the forearm roll out into full supination stretch before explosive pronation.
prerequisites: Continental grip or ability to pronate
problem.target_player: Players who get stuck in the back scratch position or push the racket straight up to the ball on their serve

symptoms.description: The racket jackknifes or travels straight up from the back scratch position toward the ball instead of flicking back and out.
Lack of explosive pronation and reduced serve power because the forearm never achieves max supination stretch.

causes.statement: The racket is directed straight up toward the ball from the back scratch instead of continuing to roll out into maximum forearm supination stretch.
Players lack kinematic awareness that the forearm is the terminal link that hits the ball, so they do not prepare the forearm to stretch and fire.
Players fixate on the back scratch position as the primary power position rather than treating it as merely a dynamic shoulder transit point.

angles.summary: The shoulder reaches max stretch at the back scratch, but the forearm reaches max supination stretch further out, preceding explosive pronation.
Vic Braden's cue: do not scratch your own back (shoulder stretch), scratch your partner's back standing beside you (forearm supination stretch).
Carlos Alcaraz, Pete Sampras, and Sabine Lisicki let the racket drift far out into supination stretch, whereas Daniil Medvedev has a more straight-over-the-top motion.
The back scratch position is commonly mistaken for the serve's max power launch position, when it is merely a random dynamic link for the forearm.

solutions.summary: Isolate forearm supination and pronation out in front of the body without raising the arm overhead or engaging the shoulder.
Perform the forearm rotation above the head with minimal shoulder involvement, visualizing an inside-to-out 'bop' action.
Chant 'Stretch, fire, stretch, fire' while rhythmically moving the racket overhead using only the forearm before introducing a ball.
Toss the ball directly over your head so it would land on your hat, and lightly bop it with forearm rotation while keeping the arm up.
solutions.external_goal: Toss the ball directly above your head/hat rather than into the court

solutions.summary: Imagine the racket is horizontal with the tip far on the inside of the hand to properly recruit the inside-out bopping roll.
solutions.external_goal: Keep racket tip on the inside of the hand before bopping

solutions.summary: Bop the tossed balls horizontally toward the baseline rather than trying to hit them down into the service box.
solutions.external_goal: Hit the bopped balls toward the baseline, not down into the service box
